Today’s highlight has to be that deadly weapon: the toast.

Last night Dad informed me that we’d leave at 7:50 this morning for haircuts. The salon wasn’t open yet when we got there, and it was too cold to wait outside, so we went into the little corner shop next door. More than ten years ago its owner lived one floor away from us. After some awkward small talk she asked where I live now. I said Germany. Her reaction was exactly the same as almost everyone’s back home, the standard routine: “Oh my, how impressive! So you’ve settled there? Is your wife there too? Everyone speaks a foreign language there, right?” Then the heart of the conversation: “So how much do you make a month? You’ve bought a place there, right?” By the time the combo was over, we had lost our spot at the front of the line: two other customers had been eyeing the salon from across the street and rushed in the second it opened. After that another five or six people trickled in. The little salon is always busy, and in the run-up to New Year it’s packed; anyone arriving later had to wait at least an hour.

“You’re So Pretty”

In the afternoon my cousin, the son of Second Aunt, one of Dad’s sisters, came home with his whole family for New Year. He and his sister have always looked out for my parents, so I told Mom and Dad that dinner today was on me, a welcome-home meal for them. More than twenty years ago, Second Aunt’s family fell into debt, and they all went to Hebei to work. Back then their greatest hope was that my cousin could become a “sales rep,” traveling around selling steel, which paid well. Within a few years he had done it, and by 2000 he was earning over 10,000 yuan a month. From then on, the family’s life changed completely. Later he went into the steel business for himself and made a lot of money. Then, just as the property market turned down, he switched to used cars, and he is now a shareholder in a nationwide chain of car dealerships. The last time we saw each other was in 2019, before the pandemic, when my family visited him in Nanjing. More than four years, gone in a flash.

The main event at dinner was the first meeting between my female cousin’s new husband and her brother. The husband is four years younger than me, eleven years younger than her and ten years younger than her brother. The new cousin-in-law isn’t much of a talker. In my parents’ words, he’s “no good”: can’t talk, doesn’t know how to work a room, doesn’t even say goodbye when he leaves. What kind of a guy is that? He was very nervous, his face flushed and dripping with sweat. My cousin was brilliant at livening things up: pouring drinks, handing out cigarettes, finding every excuse to clink glasses, attending to everyone. It had been at least seven years since I’d been in such a worldly, glad-handing scene, and I didn’t quite know what to do with myself. The most nervous person at the table was the brother-in-law; I came second. My cousin’s wife is a social operator too, and she and Mom got along famously. I took out a pack of Zhonghua and offered cigarettes around once; my cousin and the brother-in-law offered theirs to me six times. It was my first time in a cigarette-offering contest. I only took up smoking during the pandemic, and when it comes to the smoking culture of our great Zhonghua (the premium cigarette brand’s name also means “China”), I’m still a babe in arms. My role as host grew blurry; on the face of it, my cousin looked more like the host, and for a dazed moment I thought I might not have to pay today. Midway through the eating and drinking, my cousin suddenly said: “Our big scientist should propose a toast. You’re the host, you’ve got to say a few words.” My mind went blank. I tried to wriggle out of it, and at that very moment the brother-in-law found his voice: “Hey, you haven’t said anything yet!” Um. So: welcome home, brother and sister-in-law, the family together again; and congratulations, sis and brother-in-law, on your wedding—wait, it’s not a wedding—well then, here’s to a happy marriage.

What on earth did I just say? Hahaha.

I broke into a bit of a sweat. Luckily my cousin and his wife were there, and the conversation moved smoothly on to the next topic.

I’ve been home for seven days now, and I’ve noticed something interesting. When my family talks, they love restating a single point again and again, describing the same thing from every angle in different words. Take how good Second Aunt’s husband is with his hands. On that subject, every few minutes someone is likely to rediscover it: “Old Gao has such clever hands.” “Second Sister’s husband, now there’s a carpenter.” “He loves tinkering with things.”

Compliments follow the same strategy. “A big-shot PhD! As far as degrees go! A scientist! So impressive!” “Oh, I tell everyone I meet how amazing my little brother is.” “The pride of the X family!” “Always such a good boy, even as a kid…” Hearing praise like that, I can’t get a word out, only a fake smile. “Hey, bro, how much do you make a month these days?” Once they hear a number that doesn’t match their idea of a big-shot PhD and big scientist, they switch angles and praise something else: “Well, people abroad live differently from us. It’s easygoing, less pressure.”

(To be continued. Two days later, I can’t bring myself to finish it. Here instead is a drawing my cousin’s son made in 2020.)

Zhong Nanshan, the doctor who became the face of China’s fight against COVID-19: “Salute to the fighters on the front line”
